items.title: [hono] Hono: `csrf()` does not check requests sent by hyperlink auditing (`text/ping`)
items.summary: Summarycsrf() validates a request only when its Content-Type is one of the three types an HTML form can send. Chromium's hyperlink auditing (<a ping>) sends a cross-origin POST with the user's cookies and the content type text/ping, which is not in that list. The middleware does not look at Origin or Sec-Fetch-Site for such a request, so it is passed to the handler.DetailsThe middleware skips the origin check when the content type is not one that a form submission produces. The assumption was that any other content type requires a CORS preflight and therefore cannot be sent cross-origin with credentials. Hyperlink auditing is an exception: Chrome and Edge send the ping as a credentialed POST without a preflight, with a fixed body and Content-Type: text/ping.A page on another origin can therefore trigger a POST to any URL of the application. The csrf() options for origin and secFetchSite do not change the outcome, because neither header is evaluated for the request.The request body is fixed, so only actions whose effect does not depend on the body can be triggered. Firefox does not send pings by default. As with any CSRF, the user's cookie must be sent with the request, which with the default SameSite=Lax means a same-site origin or a cookie set with SameSite=None.ImpactA user who visits a malicious page in Chrome or Edge while logged in to an application protected by csrf() can be made to send a state-changing request to that application, such as logging out, deleting a resource, or toggling a setting that is selected by the path or query string.This issue affects applications that rely on csrf() as their CSRF protection and expose state-changing endpoints whose effect does not depend on the request body.WorkaroundsReject requests with a Content-Type of text/ping in a middleware registered before csrf(), or set session cookies with SameSite=Strict.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/bf16471913b5199212dac33f5d170f94745dd26ahttps://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-46wx-v44x-9hh2

items.title: [hono] Hono: `validator('form')` skips validation for `multipart/form-data` requests with extra parameters
items.summary: Summaryvalidator('form') only recognizes a multipart/form-data Content-Type that carries nothing but a single boundary parameter. A request with another legal parameter, such as charset, or with extra whitespace after the ; is not recognized as a form. The validation callback then receives an empty object, while c.req.parseBody() still parses the body as a form.DetailsThe check that decides whether a request body is a form was written as a strict pattern over the whole Content-Type value. Any parameter list that does not look exactly like ; boundary=... fails the check. When it fails, the middleware does not read the body and passes an empty object to the validation callback. If the callback accepts an empty object, the request proceeds to the handler, which can still read all submitted fields through c.req.parseBody() or c.req.formData().application/x-www-form-urlencoded is not affected. Only the multipart/form-data branch has the strict pattern.This issue arises when an application relies on validator('form') to reject or restrict fields and the validation callback does not fail on an empty object.ImpactAn unauthenticated client can send form fields that the form validator never sees, by adding a legal parameter to the Content-Type header.This may lead to:Allow-list or required-field checks in the validator being skippedFields the application intended to reject reaching the handlerThis issue affects applications that use validator('form') with multipart/form-data requests and whose validation callback accepts an empty object.WorkaroundsReject an empty object in the validator('form') callback, or validate the result of await c.req.parseBody() in the handler.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2vhttps://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/d88fab372415277a9e540e895650943dd08eef4ahttps://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4h7h-rv7c-7m2v

items.title: [hono] Hono: `mount()` and `app.mount()` can forward a path that bypasses middleware scoped inside the mount prefix
items.summary: Summarymount() and app.mount() remove the mount prefix from the request path and forward the rest to the mounted application. Two mistakes in that step let a crafted request reach a route of the mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware, such as an authentication check on /app/admin/*. The outer application routes on the original path, so the middleware does not run.DetailsDynamic prefix (all affected versions): for a mount such as /api/:tenant/*, the prefix was removed by the length of the route pattern, not of the matched prefix. A request with a longer or shorter first segment is cut in the middle, so /api/a/xxxxx/admin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.Re-normalization (since 4.12.21): the forwarded path was built from the decoded request path and assigned to url.pathname, which turns a decoded backslash into / and collapses ... /app/public%5C..%5Cadmin/secret reaches the mounted application as /admin/secret.The fix removes the prefix segment by segment from the raw pathname, using the matched parameter values for its length. Route patterns that cannot be handled safely now throw: duplicate parameter names and a wildcard inside the last segment such as /assets*. A trailing slash in an app.mount() prefix no longer removes an extra segment.ImpactAn unauthenticated client can reach a route of a mounted application that the outer application protects with path-scoped middleware.This affects applications that use mount() or app.mount() and rely on middleware registered on a sub-path inside the mount prefix for authentication or authorization.WorkaroundsRegister the authentication middleware inside the mounted application.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-4m76-xfj5-7975https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/34f90432a1794b28e52802670efcd01963f716d6https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4m76-xfj5-7975

items.title: [hono] Hono: RegExpRouter skips wildcard middleware for some route sets and for paths with an encoded line terminator
items.summary: SummaryRegExpRouter, which the default SmartRouter selects for most applications, skipped wildcard middleware in three cases, so a route handler ran without the middleware registered for it:Middleware whose parameter is written with the explicit default pattern, such as /api/:tenant{[^/]+}/admin/*, was not applied to a route written as /api/:tenant/admin/:id. (since 4.13.0)Middleware on /admin/* was not applied to a route registered on /admin* for paths under /admin/. (since 4.1.4)For a path with an encoded line terminator (%0A, %0D, %E2%80%A8, %E2%80%A9), no wildcard pattern matched, so the request reached the not-found handler without any wildcard middleware. (since 4.4.0)TrieRouter, LinearRouter and PatternRouter apply the middleware in all three cases.DetailsRegExpRouter decides at registration time which wildcard middleware covers which route. In cases 1 and 2 it treated patterns that match the same requests as different ones. In case 3 the compiled wildcard did not match line terminators.The fix derives the coverage from the structure of the registered paths and lets wildcards match line terminators. It also corrects other differences from the other routers (a wildcard in the middle of a path with parameters, duplicate middleware, middleware on static routes), and rejects custom patterns that can match the empty string, such as {[0-9]*}, with UnsupportedPathError. PreparedRegExpRouter data must be regenerated.ImpactAn unauthenticated client can reach a route handler, or the not-found handler, without the authentication or authorization middleware registered on a wildcard path.This affects applications that use RegExpRouter, directly or through the default SmartRouter, and rely on wildcard middleware for authentication or authorization.WorkaroundsUse new Hono({ router: new TrieRouter() }).Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-h7mg-cq63-vhpqhttps://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/8a103aa59bcfbffd5396b1548a0dff3688777c36https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h7mg-cq63-vhpq

items.title: [hono] Hono: `css` helper does not escape a closing tag split between the template and an interpolated value, allowing HTML injection
items.summary: SummaryThe css helper in hono/css escapes a / that follows < inside an interpolated value so that a value cannot close the <style> element. The check only looks inside each value. When the text before a value ends with <, whether that is the template itself or an earlier interpolated value, and the next value starts with /, the / is not escaped and the combined output contains an unescaped closing tag.DetailsInterpolated string values are escaped one at a time before they are joined with the surrounding template text. The rule that neutralizes </ therefore cannot see a < that belongs to the template. A template such as a content declaration that opens with a literal < and interpolates a string right after it produces a raw </style> when that string starts with /style>. During server-side rendering the <Style /> element is closed early and the rest of the value is interpreted as HTML.This issue arises only when < is the last character before an interpolation in a css template, either written in the template or supplied by a preceding value, and the interpolated value is controlled by a client.ImpactA client that controls such a value can inject HTML, including script, into the page rendered on the server.This may lead to:Execution of attacker-controlled script in the browser of a user who views the pageExposure of information available to that pageThis issue affects applications that interpolate untrusted strings into a css template immediately after a <, including two adjacent interpolations such as ${prefix}${name} where both are untrusted. Other uses of the css helper are not affected.WorkaroundsDo not interpolate untrusted values into css templates, or make sure the text before an interpolated value does not end with <.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/hono/security/advisories/GHSA-3gg2-335m-rxc6https://github.com/honojs/hono/commit/15bbd96ad1b62a0b189db4fd8dc7bf8ef280c513https://github.com/honojs/hono/releases/tag/v4.13.16https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3gg2-335m-rxc6

items.title: [@grpc/grpc-js-xds] @grpc/grpc-js: safe_regex incorrectly applies partial string matching for patterns with alternation
items.summary: SummaryThe StringMatcher/PathMatcher for safe_regex builds its RE2 as ^${regex}$ with no surrounding group. Because alternation has the lowest precedence, a pattern "a|b|c" compiles to /^a|b|c$/ -- "starts with a" OR "contains b" OR "ends with c" instead of a full match of the whole value. Configurations with safe_regex matchers that use a regex alternation (a natural way to list methods or service identities) therefore apply partial string matches. This impacts route selection, xDS credentials, and RBAC.Detailssrc/matcher.ts: SafeRegexValueMatcher and PathSafeRegexValueMatcher both dothis.targetRegexImpl = new RE2(`^${targetRegex}$`, 'u');and apply() returns targetRegexImpl.test(value). With a top-level alternation the anchors bind only to the first/last branch.https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L59https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/matcher.ts#L232src/route.ts (getPredicateForStringMatcher / getPredicateForHeaderMatcher) builds these for every safe_regex StringMatcher/HeaderMatcher, and src/rbac.ts uses them for RBAC url_path permissions/principals, authenticated.principal_name (mTLS SAN/CN), requested_server_name and header rules. So an ALLOW rule written with an alternation grants access to method names, certificate identities or header values that extend an intended one. DENY policies only become broader (fail-safe).https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L28https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/e742b11bd8039f3dbea4cd29afdf5d95a8ba6b92/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/route.ts#L47Proof of conceptIn a scratch directory:npm init -ynpm i @grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.1 @grpc/grpc-jsnode poc.cjspoc.cjs calls the exported RBAC engine directly (the functions grpc-js uses to make the authorization decision); no server or network:const { parseConfig } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/rbac.js')const { SafeRegexValueMatcher } = require('@grpc/grpc-js-xds/build/src/matcher.js')const { Metadata } = require('@grpc/grpc-js')console.log(new SafeRegexValueMatcher('admin|editor').toString()) // SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u)const sr = regex => ({ match_pattern: 'safe_regex', safe_regex: { regex } })const info = urlPath => ({ urlPath, headers: new Metadata(), tls: true, peerCertificate: null,  destinationIp: '10.0.0.1', destinationPort: 443, sourceIp: '10.0.0.2' })const g = parseConfig({ action: 'ALLOW', policies: { p: {  permissions: [{ rule: 'url_path', url_path: { path: sr('/acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers') } }],  principals: [{ identifier: 'any', any: true }] } } })console.log('GetUser       ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUser')))       // true  (intended)console.log('DeleteUser    ', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/DeleteUser')))    // false (control)console.log('GetUserSecrets', g.apply(info('/acme.Users/GetUserSecrets'))) // true <-- BYPASSObserved (grpc-js-xds 1.14.1, grpc-js 1.14.6):matcher "admin|editor" -> SafeRegex(/^admin|editor$/u);    apply("administrator")=true, apply("not-an-editor")=trueALLOW url_path /acme.Users/GetUser|/acme.Users/ListUsers:    /acme.Users/GetUser         -> ALLOWED (intended)    /acme.Users/DeleteUser      -> denied  (control)    /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets  -> ALLOWED <-- bypass (policy intends deny)control, same regex as (?:...|...): /acme.Users/GetUserSecrets -> deniedALLOW authenticated principal_name spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend|...ops/sa/admin:    spiffe://prod/ns/web/sa/frontend-batch -> ALLOWED <-- bypassImpactUsers of @grpc/grpc-js-xds who are using safe_regex matchers with alternation for route selection, xDS credentials SAN matchers, or RBAC rules may see incorrectly permissive behavior.Referenceshttps://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/security/advisories/GHSA-r7hq-q2xm-6c5mhttps://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/commit/3fc3b0ebf7a89d64843a73679951142d33b40cb1https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/commit/57a67e96babcb29b6eabc1833221ccf2fa152d43https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/releases/tag/@grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.13.2https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/releases/tag/@grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r7hq-q2xm-6c5m

items.title: [@grpc/grpc-js-xds] @grpc/grpc-js: RBAC override configs in VirtualHost and Route resources are not applied
items.summary: SummaryXdsServer in @grpc/grpc-js-xds does not apply RBACPerRoute overrides from matching Route or VirtualHost resources. When a trusted xDS control plane supplies a broad top-level ALLOW policy and a stricter override, XdsServer ACKs the resources but evaluates the RPC under the top-level policy.DetailsOverride parser lookup uses the override message typeparseOverrideFilterConfig() in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts:225-257 looks up FILTER_REGISTRY using the override message type:type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRouteSource: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter.ts#L225-L257setup() in packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts:167-173 registers the filter only under the top-level RBAC type:type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACSource: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/http-filter/rbac-filter.ts#L167-L173The lookup returns null even though the registered entry contains parseOverrideRbacConfig(), and server.ts silently skips the override.Override maps are keyed by type URL instead of filter nameoverrideConfigMaps in server.ts:99-102 is documented as keyed by HTTP filter name, but server.ts:169-174 stores each map under filterConfig.typeUrl.Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L99-L102Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L169-L174Route overrides are later looked up by their typed_per_filter_config key, which is the HttpFilter.name. An ordinary key such as rbac therefore misses the stored map.VirtualHost overrides are not readhandleRouteConfigurationResource() in server.ts:225-249 reads route.typed_per_filter_config but never reads virtualHost.typed_per_filter_config.Source: https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/blob/56567d9604b4e45cdca0d2e3c2a60ac227ee659d/packages/grpc-js-xds/src/server.ts#L225-L249When no override reaches the RBAC interceptor, rbac-filter.ts:125-155 evaluates the broader top-level policy.Proof of conceptSet:GRPC_XDS_EXPERIMENTAL_RBAC=trueRun XdsServer with a protected unary handler.Have the ADS control plane deliver a Listener containing an RBAC HTTP filter named rbac with a top-level ALLOW-any policy:name: rbactyped_config:  "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBAC  rules:    action: ALLOW    policies:      allow-any:        principals: [{ any: true }]        permissions: [{ any: true }]Deliver a matching non-forwarding route with this override:typed_per_filter_config:  rbac:    "@type": type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.rbac.v3.RBACPerRoute    rbac:      rules:        action: DENY        policies:          deny-any:            principals: [{ any: true }]            permissions: [{ any: true }]Invoke the protected unary method without credentials.Expected: The route-specific DENY policy rejects the RPC before the protected handler runs.Observed: XdsServer ACKs the resources, retains the top-level ALLOW policy, and runs the protected handler.Listener and RouteConfiguration: ACKEDgRPC status: OKhandler invocations: 1response: PROTECTED_SECRET_RECORD_RBAC_OVERRIDEImpactUsers of @grpc/grpc-js-xds who are using RBAC-based authentication with override configurations may unintentionally accept some requests that should be rejected.Referenceshttps://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/security/advisories/GHSA-gg5j-6742-v827https://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/commit/b8f3ced4d4699338dd33dc0f7b1d68d689a31d0ehttps://github.com/grpc/grpc-node/releases/tag/@grpc/grpc-js-xds@1.14.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-gg5j-6742-v827

items.title: [@astrojs/solid-js] Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/solid-js
items.summary:
SummaryThe @astrojs/solid-js renderer wraps named slot content passed to Solid components in an element, and writes the slot name into its name attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing " could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page.For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request:---import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.jsx';const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab');---
…
rendered with a Solid component that renders a slot by name:export default function Tabs(props) { return
{props[props.active]}
;}would output a tab value such as x"> as live HTML.ImpactReflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true:The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name.The Solid component is hydrated with a client:* directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its name attribute.The Solid component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means accessing slot props by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template.This is the @astrojs/solid-js counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in astro core.Affected versions@astrojs/solid-js >= 0.2.0, <= 7.1.1.PatchesFixed in @astrojs/solid-js 7.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer.WorkaroundsUpgrade to @astrojs/solid-js 7.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component.CreditsReported by @manus-pi.Referenceshttps://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-jmv2-qgxf-f995https://github.com/withastro/astro/commit/290b196ddb48de11783ff128e2b7272c61490a20https://github.com/withastro/astro/releases/tag/@astrojs/solid-js@7.1.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jmv2-qgxf-f995

items.title: [@astrojs/svelte] Astro: Reflected XSS via unescaped slot names in @astrojs/svelte
items.summary:
SummaryThe @astrojs/svelte renderer wraps slotted content passed to Svelte components in an element, and writes the slot name into its name attribute without HTML escaping. A slot name containing " could end the attribute and inject arbitrary HTML into the page.For example, a page that takes a slot name from the request:---import Tabs from '../components/Tabs.svelte';const tab = Astro.url.searchParams.get('tab');---
…
rendered with a Svelte 5 component that renders its snippets by name:{@render snippets[active]?.()}would output a tab value such as x"> as live HTML.ImpactReflected cross-site scripting. An attacker who gets a user to open a crafted link can run JavaScript on the site's origin, but only in applications where all of the following are true:The page passes request-controlled input (such as a query parameter) as a slot name.The Svelte component is hydrated with a client:* directive. For non-hydrated components the slot wrapper is removed from the output, together with its name attribute.The Svelte component renders the attacker-chosen slot, which in practice means a Svelte 5 component that renders snippets by a dynamic name. Components that never render the slot only output Astro's already escaped fallback template.This is the @astrojs/svelte counterpart of GHSA-8hv8-536x-4wqp (CVE-2026-50146), which fixed the same issue in astro core. The same unescaped value was also used when hydrating the component in the browser.Affected versions@astrojs/svelte >= 5.7.3, <= 9.1.1.PatchesFixed in @astrojs/svelte 9.1.2. Slot names are now HTML-escaped in the server renderer and in the client-side hydration code.WorkaroundsUpgrade to @astrojs/svelte 9.1.2 or later. Before upgrading, do not use request-controlled input as a slot name, or map it to a fixed set of known slot names before passing it to a component.CreditsReported by @manus-pi.Referenceshttps://github.com/withastro/astro/security/advisories/GHSA-f4j9-crrj-867qhttps://github.com/withastro/astro/commit/5e476365378e41aa2745d003b2383d02008d7b44https://github.com/withastro/astro/releases/tag/@astrojs/svelte@9.1.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f4j9-crrj-867q

items.title: [basic-ftp] basic-ftp: Uncaught exception crashes the Node.js process when a password (or resumed-download path) contains CR/LF
items.summary:
SummaryClient.login() calls FTPContext.send() from inside the control-socket data event handler. send() throws on CR, LF or NUL, and nothing catches the throw. A password containing 
 therefore raises an uncaught exception and terminates the whole Node.js process. It does not reject the returned promise. Any application that passes untrusted input as the FTP password can be crashed remotely with one request. The same pattern exists in the REST/RETR path of downloadTo() when the remote path contains control characters.DetailsThe CRLF guard (FTPContext.send, src/FtpContext.ts ~L233) correctly refuses to send commands containing , 
 or \0:send(command: string) {    if (/[
\0]/.test(command)) {        throw new Error(`Invalid command: Contains control characters. (${command})`);    }That works when send() is called from handle(), because it runs inside a Promise executor and the throw becomes a rejection. But in two places send() runs inside a response handler, which is called synchronously from the socket’s data event:Client.login() (src/Client.ts ~L246-248): after the server answers 331 to USER, the handler calls this.ftp.send("PASS " + password). The USER command was already sent and is valid, so the password is only checked at this point. The call chain is socket.on("data") → _onControlSocketData → _passToHandler → responseHandler → send() → throw. No try/catch exists anywhere in that chain, so it becomes an uncaughtException.downloadTo() (src/transfer.ts ~L368-370): when startAt > 0, the initial command is REST n, which contains no user-controlled text. When the server answers 350, the handler calls config.ftp.send("RETR " + config.remotePath). This remotePath was never checked before. A path with a control character throws in the data handler in the same way. (Found by code reading, not reproduced.)Because the exception happens during data event dispatch, it can’t be handled with try/catch or .catch() around client.access() or downloadTo(). The application only survives if it has a global process.on("uncaughtException") handler.Proof of conceptTested on Node.js v22.22.0 against basic-ftp 6.2.2 (built from source). It uses a minimal mock FTP server on localhost:const net = require("net")const ftp = require("basic-ftp")const srv = net.createServer(s => {  s.write("220 hi
")  s.on("data", d => {    const c = d.toString()    if (c.startsWith("USER")) s.write("331 pw
")    else if (c.startsWith("PASS")) s.write("230 ok
")    else s.write("200 ok
")  })})srv.listen(0, async () => {  const c = new ftp.Client(2000)  try {    await c.access({      host: "127.0.0.1",      port: srv.address().port,      user: "bob",      password: "x
DELE important"   // attacker-controlled value    })  } catch (e) {    console.log("rejected:", e.message)  // never reached  }  console.log("handled gracefully")      // never reached  process.exit(0)})Result: the process terminates with an uncaught exception and neither catch nor the final console.log runs:Error: Invalid command: Contains control characters. (PASS xDELE important)    at FTPContext.send (dist/FtpContext.js:189:19)    at Object.responseHandler (dist/Client.js:186:26)    at FTPContext._passToHandler (dist/FtpContext.js:322:24)    at FTPContext._onControlSocketData (dist/FtpContext.js:312:18)    at Socket.<anonymous> (dist/FtpContext.js:133:44)The server in the PoC is benign. Any normal FTP server that replies 331 to USER triggers the same crash.ImpactDenial of service (uncaught exception, process termination), CWE-248.It affects applications that pass untrusted or user-influenced values as the FTP password, or as the remote path of a resumed download. Examples are web apps or services that let users enter their own FTP credentials, or file-transfer or backup tools driven by user-supplied paths. One request crashes the whole Node.js process and every other client it serves. It needs no authentication to the FTP server and no special server behaviour. The attacker only needs control over the string. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected, and the CRLF guard still blocks command injection.Suggested fix:In FTPContext._passToHandler(), wrap the handler call in a try/catch that rejects the task and calls closeWithError(err).Validate password in login(), and remotePath in _downloadToStream(), before any I/O and reject early.Referenceshttps://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/security/advisories/GHSA-r4jh-29pc-gfqrhttps://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/commit/0495b906bdf891e68806721b07b333dba65ec88ehttps://github.com/patrickjuchli/basic-ftp/releases/tag/v6.2.3https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r4jh-29pc-gfqr

items.title: [basic-ftp] basic-ftp: Uncaught TypeError in MLSD directory-listing parser via __proto__ fact name causes DoS in Client.list()
items.summary:
Summarybasic-ftp's MLSD directory-listing parser (src/parseListMLSD.ts) looks up fact-handler functions in a plain object literal keyed directly by fact names taken from the FTP server's response, with no validation. A directory-listing line containing the fact name "proto" resolves this lookup to Object.prototype (inherited, non-own, non-function) instead of undefined, so the "not a function" guard is bypassed and the code throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.This TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is not caught by Client.list()'s retry logic and propagates as a rejected promise out of list() and every API built on top of it (list, downloadToDir, uploadFromDir, clearWorkingDir, removeDir). Any FTP server the client connects to — or any on-path attacker on a plaintext (non-TLS) FTP session — can crash the calling application by returning one crafted line in a directory listing. If the application does not wrap every one of these calls in try/catch, the rejection is unhandled and crashes the Node.js process (default behavior since Node 15).DetailsFile: src/parseListMLSD.tsconst factHandlersByName: {[key: string]: FactHandler} = {    "size": parseSize,    "sizd": parseSize,    "unique": (value, info) => { info.uniqueID = value },    "modify": (value, info) => { ... },    "type": (value, info) => { ... },    "unix.mode": (value, info) => { ... },    ...}export function parseLine(line: string): FileInfo | undefined {    const [ packedFacts, name ] = splitStringOnce(line, " ")    ...    const facts = packedFacts.split(";")    for (const fact of facts) {        const [ factName, factValue ] = splitStringOnce(fact, "=")        if (!factValue) { continue }        const factHandler = factHandlersByName[factName.toLowerCase()]   // <-- unsafe lookup        if (!factHandler) { continue }        const result = factHandler(factValue, info)                     // <-- throws here        ...    }    return info}factHandlersByName is a plain {} object literal, so it inherits from Object.prototype. Property access does not distinguish own keys from inherited ones. When factName.toLowerCase() === "proto", the bracket lookup factHandlersByName["proto"] returns Object.prototype itself — a truthy, non-undefined value — so the if (!factHandler) continue guard does not fire. The code then tries to call Object.prototype as a function: factHandler(factValue, info), which throws TypeError: factHandler is not a function.This line runs inside parseList() (src/parseList.ts), called synchronously from a .map() over every line of the listing, which in turn is called from Client._requestListWithCommand() -> Client.list() (src/Client.ts). list()'s only error handling is:    catch (err) {        const shouldTryNext = err instanceof FTPError        if (!shouldTryNext) { throw err }        lastError = err    }A plain TypeError is not an FTPError, so it is immediately rethrown instead of being retried or suppressed, and the Promise returned by list() rejects with it.Affected call paths (all eventually call Client.list()):Client.list()Client.downloadToDir() / _downloadFromWorkingDir()Client.clearWorkingDir()Client.removeDir()Only "proto" triggers the crash this way; other reserved Object.prototype property names tested ("constructor", "toString", "hasOwnProperty", "valueOf", "defineGetter") happen to resolve to actual functions on Object.prototype, so they are called without throwing (silently ineffective, not a crash). items.title: [@hono/node-server] @hono/node-server: Unhandled `ECONNRESET` on the socket during an asynchronous WebSocket upgrade crashes the process
items.summary: SummaryWhile @hono/node-server waits for the Hono application to handle a WebSocket upgrade request, the socket has no error listener. If the client resets the TCP connection during that time, the resulting ECONNRESET is emitted as an unhandled 'error' event and the process terminates.DetailsThe upgrade handler awaits the application before attaching any listener to the socket. When middleware on the upgrade path does asynchronous work, such as an authentication lookup, a connection reset in that window has no handler. If a global uncaughtException handler swallows the error, the pending upgrade is never released and its entry is retained for the lifetime of the process.The fix attaches error and close listeners to the socket before calling the application, releases the pending upgrade when the socket closes, and skips the handshake on a destroyed socket.ImpactAn unauthenticated client can terminate the server process with a single connection by sending a WebSocket upgrade request and resetting the connection before the application has responded. Where the crash is suppressed, repeated requests grow the heap.This affects applications that enable WebSocket support in @hono/node-server and run asynchronous middleware or handlers on the upgrade path.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/node-server/security/advisories/GHSA-qv5m-9pm6-hqp3https://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/61cc0267e613e684401f17c27538ba3bf97339a4https://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v2.1.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qv5m-9pm6-hqp3

items.title: [@hono/node-server] @hono/node-server: Backslash in the request path is parsed as a path separator, bypassing path-based access control at a reverse proxy
items.summary: Summary@hono/node-server passes the raw request-target to the WHATWG URL parser, which treats a backslash in the path as / and then resolves .. segments. A request for /admin\secret or /public\..\admin/secret reaches the application as /admin/secret. A reverse proxy that follows RFC 3986 forwards the backslash unchanged and applies its path-based rules to the original path, so the request reaches a route the proxy is meant to block.DetailsA raw backslash is not allowed in a request-target (RFC 3986, RFC 9112 Section 3.2.1), and RFC 9112 Section 3.2 says a recipient should reject such a request rather than correct it. Proxies such as nginx on Linux, HAProxy and Envoy keep the backslash as an ordinary character, so they and the application see different paths.The fix responds with 400 Bad Request to a request whose path contains a raw backslash, for HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, absolute-form request-targets and WebSocket upgrades. A percent-encoded backslash and a backslash in the query string are still accepted.ImpactAn unauthenticated client can reach a route that a reverse proxy, load balancer or WAF in front of the application blocks by path.This affects applications served by @hono/node-server behind a front component that makes path-based decisions and forwards a backslash unchanged. Access control inside the Hono application, such as middleware on /admin/*, runs on the rewritten path and is not affected.Referenceshttps://github.com/honojs/node-server/security/advisories/GHSA-jpvv-r467-5p4whttps://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/3868998a805ae79216535ad3986c1e7228dee313https://github.com/honojs/node-server/commit/fb97395ec36af66567c76976e741110b02804d1chttps://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v1.19.18https://github.com/honojs/node-server/releases/tag/v2.1.6https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jpvv-r467-5p4w
